title: Bhishma's vow
carry: a vow with witnesses is hard to take back

segments.voice: Yesterday in Bhishma's vow: a father's half answer, and a son who quietly found the other half — a true reason, not the whole one. Did you ask someone one more gentle question? Day seven hundred twelve.
screen: `A TRUE REASON, NOT THE WHOLE ONE.`

segments.voice: The heir to the throne comes to a fisherman's door, and he doesn't come alone. Devavrata brings old chiefs of the warrior class with him, elders whose word carries weight. He has come on his father's errand: to ask for the fisherman's daughter as a bride for the king. The fisherman receives them with honor. And then, politely, carefully, with all those elders listening, he tells the prince exactly what's wrong with the match.
screen: `A PRINCE AT A FISHERMAN'S DOOR.` → `ELDERS AS WITNESSES.` → `WHAT'S WRONG WITH THE MATCH.`

segments.voice: The fisherman starts with praise. This match, he says, is one anyone would want; to turn it down would be foolish. He has no quarrel with the king. But there is one fault, and he names it: a rival. Whoever has you as a rival, he tells Devavrata, god or demon, can never live happily for long. That's a bold thing to say. A fisherman, speaking to a warrior prince, the king's own heir, in front of witnesses, is saying, in effect: the problem is you. Your strength. Your claim. Any grandson of his would grow up in that shadow. And Devavrata doesn't argue. He doesn't say he'd never harm a child, or ask to be trusted. He answers the problem by removing it. Hear my vow, he says, before all these chiefs. The son born of her will be our king. I give up the throne. The place he gives up is heir apparent, yuvaraja, the one his father gave him when he brought him home from the river. A few days ago in our reading, we watched Shantanu make him heir. Now, for his father's happiness, he hands it away to a brother who isn't even born. Notice where he speaks it. Not in private, not to his father, but in a fisherman's house, before elders who can hold him to it. A vow with witnesses is hard to take back, and he seems to want it that way. And the fisherman listens, and thanks him. Then he says there's one more thing he's worried about. That's tomorrow.
screen: `THE FISHERMAN'S PRAISE.` · `ONE FAULT: A RIVAL.` · `THE PROBLEM IS YOU.` · `I GIVE UP THE THRONE.` · then, large: `A VOW WITH WITNESSES.`

segments.voice: Let your shoulders soften and the breath slow down. Bring to mind something that's yours: a seat, a title, a turn, a habit of being first. Not something you'd lose in an emergency. Just something you're used to holding. Picture it in your closed hand. Breathe in, and feel how naturally you hold it. Breathe out, and imagine opening the hand, just slightly. You don't have to give anything up. Only notice what the open hand feels like. The bell holds the time.
Bhishma's vow. Its first part: before the elders, Devavrata gives up the throne so a fisherman's grandson can have it.
Your line: a vow with witnesses is hard to take back. Today, give up one small thing that's yours so someone else can have it. Day seven hundred twelve.

original.note: Sanskrit yuvarāja, the heir apparent: the place Shantanu gave Devavrata, and the place he gives up.

trapdoor: what you thought: Bhishma's vow is one promise.
what it means: it begins with a first promise, giving up the throne, spoken before witnesses.
what a scholar hears: the fisherman names Devavrata as the rival, and the first vow is made before aged warrior chiefs.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Devavrata and the elders at the fisherman's house; the fisherman's objection; the first vow)

notes: All paraphrase. Check: Devavrata goes with aged Kshatriya chiefs; the fisherman's praise of the match; his naming of a rival as the one objection.
'A few days ago in our reading' refers to day 709 of this serial, not to time in the story (Ganguli has years pass between the installation and the Yamuna).
The fisherman's speech in Ganguli also mentions Satyavati's birth father and a sage who sought her; left out here; her birth is told on day 716.
yuvaraja is used for the heir-apparent role; confirm the term matches the Sanskrit of the passage.
Editor (y3 audit): replaced 'Think about how bold that is' (banned hook-style opener); yuvaraja is now given as the name of the role, not as a claim about the passage's Sanskrit.
